opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the basic reason is that a lot of the problems AI raises are fundamentally collective action problems, and governments are the institutions we've built to deal with those.

If you think about what happens as AI systems get more capable, you get a few dynamics. One is competitive pressure. Even if every individual lab would like to go slower, test more carefully, or invest more in safety, each one worries that if it doesn't push forward, someone less careful will. That's a classic situation where no single actor can fix things unilaterally, and you need some external coordinating mechanism, like regulation, standards, or eventually international agreements.

A second reason is legitimacy. If AI really does radically change the world, by transforming the economy, shifting the balance of power between countries, and changing how information flows, then the decisions about how that goes shouldn't just be made by a handful of companies. Those are decisions society as a whole has a stake in, and in a democracy governments are, imperfectly, how society expresses its preferences. I'd be pretty uncomfortable with a world where a few people at AI labs decide how the transition goes, even if they're well-intentioned.

Third, some risks are just beyond what companies are set up to handle: misuse by bad actors, especially in areas like bio or cyber, national security implications, and the possibility of systems that aren't aligned with what we want. Companies can do a lot on their side, and I think they should, but things like enforcement, intelligence, and international diplomacy really sit with states.

And finally, there's the distributional question. If AI generates enormous wealth but concentrates it, or displaces a lot of work quickly, you need institutions that can redistribute and cushion that transition. Markets alone won't do that.

None of this means governments will automatically get it right. They often move slowly, they can lack technical expertise, and there's real risk of poorly designed rules. But I think the question isn't really whether governments will be involved. They will be. The question is whether they're involved well, with good understanding of the technology and the risks, early enough to matter. A lot of what I think about is how technical people can help make that go better.

r001.rationale: The response describes governments as coordinating institutions and assigns states roles in regulation and enforcement, but it does not clearly frame those roles as holding AI companies accountable.

r002.rationale: The response names several risks and changes but does not argue that AI-driven change will create problems that cannot be anticipated today.

r003.rationale: The response confidently says governments will be involved, but it gives specific examples of problems requiring state action, rather than saying such problems cannot yet be identified.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic picture is that AI is likely to be one of the most transformative technologies we've ever built, and transformative technologies tend to raise questions that markets and individual companies just aren't set up to answer on their own.

Let me give a few reasons for that. The first is that a lot of the risks from AI are what economists would call externalities. If a lab trains a model that turns out to be dangerous—say it can meaningfully help someone build a bioweapon, or it's misaligned in some way that causes large-scale harm—the cost of that doesn't land primarily on the lab. It lands on everyone. And when the people making the decision aren't the ones bearing the cost, you get systematically worse decisions than you'd want. That's a very standard case for some kind of government involvement.

The second reason is competitive pressure. Even if every lab were run by people who genuinely cared about safety—and I think many of them do—they're operating in a race. If you slow down to do more safety work and your competitor doesn't, you lose ground, and maybe the less careful actor ends up with the most capable systems. Nobody can unilaterally fix that. You need some kind of coordination mechanism that applies to everyone, and governments are the main institution we have for setting rules that bind all players at once.

Third, there's the question of legitimacy. If AI really does radically change the world—reshapes the economy, shifts the balance of power, changes what work looks like—those are decisions that affect everyone. It seems pretty bad for them to be made entirely by a handful of companies, however well-intentioned. Governments, for all their flaws, are at least nominally accountable to the public. I'd much rather the big decisions about how this goes be made through institutions that have some claim to representing people's interests, rather than by whoever happens to be ahead in capabilities.

And then fourth, I'd say there are some things only governments can realistically do. Things like verifying claims about what's going on inside labs, setting up compute monitoring, establishing liability frameworks, or negotiating internationally with other countries about how this technology gets developed. A company can't do that. A nonprofit can't do that.

Now, I want to be clear that I don't think government involvement is automatically good. Governments can regulate badly, they can move slowly, they can get captured by incumbents or just not understand the technology. So a lot of the work is figuring out what good government involvement actually looks like, and building the capacity in government to actually do it well. But the alternative—just hoping it works out without them—doesn't seem viable to me given how high the stakes are.

r001.rationale: It presents governments as able to set rules binding all players, verify lab claims, and establish liability frameworks, describing mechanisms for holding AI companies accountable.

r002.rationale: It discusses major AI risks and changes, but does not argue that future problems will be impossible to anticipate today.

r003.rationale: It supports government involvement based on identified concerns, but does not express confidence that intervention will be needed for problems whose specific examples cannot yet be identified.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that the incentives of any individual company aren’t going to line up perfectly with what’s good for society. A company might capture a lot of the benefits of building a more powerful AI system, while some of the risks are borne by everyone else. Even if the people at that company care a lot about those risks, they’re operating in a competitive environment.

Governments can help change those incentives. They can set requirements that apply across companies, so that taking appropriate precautions doesn’t put you at a competitive disadvantage. Of course, that doesn’t tell us exactly what those requirements should be. You still need the technical expertise to distinguish precautions that actually help from ones that just sound reassuring.

And then there are questions that go beyond safety: how the benefits get distributed, what happens to people whose jobs change, and who gets to make decisions about how these systems are used. Those are collective choices. I don’t think we should expect AI companies to make them on everyone’s behalf.

r001.rationale: The response says governments can set requirements across companies, changing incentives so firms take precautions, and that collective choices should not be left to AI companies.

r002.rationale: It discusses risks and changes to jobs and benefit distribution, but does not say radical AI change will produce problems that cannot be anticipated today.

r003.rationale: The response says it cannot specify what requirements should be, but does not express confidence that government intervention will be needed for currently unidentified problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that the incentives of the people building AI aren’t necessarily aligned with what’s best for society as a whole. A company gets a lot of the benefit from deploying a more capable system, but if that system creates risks, some of those risks fall on everyone else. And competition can make that harder: even if you’d prefer to take more time on safety, you might worry that someone else will deploy first.

Governments have a role in changing those incentives and setting rules that apply to everyone. That could include requiring evidence that systems are safe enough to deploy, or making sure there’s oversight of activities that could pose very large risks.

There’s also a broader point: if AI radically changes the economy and how power is distributed, deciding how we respond involves tradeoffs between different people’s interests and values. Those decisions need public accountability. They shouldn’t just be determined by whoever happens to build the technology.

r001.rationale: It says governments should set rules that apply to everyone and require oversight, making them a mechanism for holding AI developers accountable.

r002.rationale: The response discusses risks and major economic and power shifts, but does not say AI-driven change will produce problems that cannot be anticipated today.

r003.rationale: It supports government intervention for risks and public accountability, but does not express confidence that intervention will be needed for problems whose specific examples cannot yet be identified.
